title: What is a personal investing agent?
summary: A personal investing agent is AI that connects to your accounts, watches what you own, and tells you what matters. You make every decision.
body_markdown:
## How is it different from a robo-advisor, a chatbot or a human adviser?


It overlaps with four things people already use.


### How is it different from a robo-advisor?


The SEC describes a robo-advisor as an automated advisory program that asks you about your goals, time horizon and risk tolerance, then creates and manages an investment portfolio for you. You open an account with the robo-advisor, and it manages the portfolio based on your answers. That’s a good fit if you want to hand over the day-to-day decisions.


A personal investing agent is built for the opposite preference. Your money stays in the accounts you already have, you keep choosing your own investments, and the agent doesn’t rebalance, trade or manage anything on its own. More in[robo-advisor vs. AI investing agent vs. financial advisor](https://www.astor.app/blog/robo-advisor-vs-ai-investing-agent-vs-financial-advisor) ,[Astor vs. Wealthfront](https://www.astor.app/blog/astor-vs-wealthfront) and[Astor vs. Betterment](https://www.astor.app/blog/astor-vs-betterment) .


### How is it different from ChatGPT or another AI chatbot?


General chatbots have gotten closer. In the US, ChatGPT’s Finances feature can connect your accounts through Plaid and review your allocation, and Perplexity lets users in the US and Canada link brokerage accounts through Plaid too. Both can send you updates, mostly through scheduled tasks and alerts you set up yourself.


Two differences remain. A chatbot is general-purpose, so watching your portfolio is something you configure rather than the thing it’s for. And OpenAI says ChatGPT isn’t a fiduciary or a registered investment adviser, while Perplexity says its finance data isn’t investment advice. When a personal investing agent is offered by a registered investment adviser, its recommendations are personalized advice and the firm owes you a fiduciary duty. More in[Astor vs. ChatGPT](https://www.astor.app/blog/astor-vs-chatgpt) and[Astor vs. Perplexity Finance](https://www.astor.app/blog/astor-vs-perplexity-finance) .


### How is it different from your brokerage’s AI assistant?


Some brokerages now build an assistant into their app. Robinhood’s Cortex, for example, is available to Robinhood Gold members ($5 a month) and can give portfolio insights, monitor market moves and news that may affect your portfolio, and prepare orders that you review and submit. Robinhood says Cortex can’t give buy or sell recommendations and isn’t an investment adviser.


A brokerage assistant lives inside that brokerage’s app, so if you also have a 401(k) or crypto elsewhere, it sees only one piece of the picture. A personal investing agent sits across all of your accounts. More in[AI investing apps that work with your brokerage](https://www.astor.app/blog/ai-investing-apps-that-work-with-your-brokerage) .


### How is it different from a human financial adviser?


A human investment adviser gives ongoing advice about buying, selling and holding investments, monitors how your investments line up with your goals, and often offers financial planning too, according to the SEC’s Investor.gov. Registered advisers are required to act in your best interest. A good adviser brings judgment about your whole life, from taxes and estate planning to the hard choices where you want a person to talk to. A personal investing agent doesn’t replace that.


What an agent offers is narrower. It follows every position you own and reaches you by text when something matters. Investor.gov notes that advisers’ fees are typically based on the value of the assets in your account, while Astor charges a flat subscription. If you want a person, a human adviser is the right choice, and if you want to keep making your own decisions with something watching what you own, an agent fits. More on costs in[how much an AI financial advisor costs](https://www.astor.app/blog/ai-financial-advisor-cost) .
